This sentence construction is a frequent point of debate in American English. It's very old-fashioned. Today, it's usually not used and is considered grammatically incorrect by many.
|The house was built in 1907; the whole town was rebuilt.||
Many Americans are still using it, but the preferred structure is:
|The town was rebuilt in 1907; the house was built then.||
Why is "the whole town was rebuilt" sometimes criticized?
The original sentence implies that "the town" is rebuilt in the same year as the construction of "the house." The structure is ambiguous. By putting "the house was built in 1907" and "the whole town was rebuilt" in separate clauses, you suggest the town was rebuilt around that time, not necessarily that the house was part of the rebuilding process in 1907.

Here is a comprehensive guide to the common myths about HIV and AIDS, debunked with scientific facts and the current understanding of the virus.

---

## 1. What is HIV?
Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) is a virus that targets the immune system's white blood cells, specifically the T-cells, which are vital for fighting infection. When HIV invades and begins to damage or destroy these cells, the immune system's ability to fight off other illnesses is impaired.
This condition eventually becomes AIDS when the immune system's function is so severely damaged that the body is unable to fight off other infections and diseases, particularly those related to the immune system.
